One demonstration closer to delivering VIPER to the Moon.
 
We just completed a risk-reduction test campaign with @NASA: running a full offload with a VIPER Mobility Ground Research Unit (MGRU) before doing so on the lunar surface.
 
We proved out the full concept of operations with our flight-like offloader: the complete offload sequence, nominal and off-nominal, ran end-to-end across the full range of lander tilt angles, with joint mission operations and NASA commanding the rover remotely. Stay tuned for images of our flight offloader, which is being fabricated now!

New Glenn 9x4 has been added to NASA’s Launch Services Program, making both New Glenn configurations eligible to compete for NASA science and exploration missions.

With an 8.7-meter fairing and the ability to carry more than 70 metric tons to LEO, 9x4 gives NASA greater payload capacity and flexibility as we expand the New Glenn fleet 🚀

Two paths to orbit. More flexibility for NASA.

Power changes what’s possible on the lunar surface.

Our Power Tower is a 20-meter-tall, vertically deployed solar array system designed to provide more than 10 kilowatts of power for Moon Base operations at the lunar South Pole. Its modular architecture will support future surface networks, extending power beyond the lander to the assets that need it most.

28.1 miles on Mars, powered by Rocket Lab hardware.

NASA's Perseverance rover has now driven 28.1 miles (45.2 km) across the Red Planet in just five and a half years, breaking an off-world driving record that took Opportunity nearly 15 years to set.

Rocket Lab solar panels powered Perseverance's cruise to Mars, then on the surface, Rocket Lab Robotics (formerly Motiv Space Systems) hardware helps turn those miles into science — from the Mastcam-Z camera mechanisms that zoom in on targets, to the 7-foot robotic arm placing instruments against Martian rock with sub-millimeter precision.

Every mile is another step in the search for signs of ancient life.

🚀 VA271 – LE-04 : Ariane 6's 10th flight is on the horizon!

Arianespace is preparing to launch 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard Ariane 64 from Europe's Spaceport in French Guiana. Liftoff is currently targeted for no earlier than November 23.

This will be the fourth Ariane 6 mission for Amazon Leo, bringing the total number of satellites launched by Arianespace for the constellation to 136, upon successful completion.

For this mission, Ariane 6 will fly in its most powerful configuration, with four P160C solid rocket boosters.

Another step in Ariane 6's operational ramp-up and our continued partnership with Amazon to help bring connectivity to more people around the world.

#LaunchingAmbitions #Ariane6
@AmazonLeo

When can we call a mission a success? 🚀

Liftoff may be the most spectacular moment, but it’s only the beginning.

For Arianespace, success means delivering a spacecraft where it needs to be, with the right trajectory and the right conditions for separation.

Once the spacecraft has safely separated from the launcher, it can begin the next part of its journey, whether that means reaching its operational orbit, deploying its systems or travelling towards a much more distant destination.

That’s where our launch mission ends, and our customer’s mission begins.

#LaunchingAmbitions

🚀 Before a spacecraft can be launched, it first has to arrive at Europe’s Spaceport.

Travelling by sea or air in a specially designed transport container, the spacecraft is taken to the Payload Preparation Complex, where its launch campaign begins.

Inside a controlled clean-room environment, teams open the container and carry out a series of inspections to confirm that the spacecraft has arrived in the expected condition.

From there, Arianespace coordinates the different stages of the launch campaign through to liftoff.

✔️ Structural steel on the east side of the launch table is complete.

September was a big month for test operations across our sites.

📍 NASA Stennis, MS
Stage 2 completed its first wet dress rehearsal! The team put the stage through flight-like propellant loading, COPV fills, engine chill operations, and a simulated stage 1 ascent timeline, building toward its first integrated hot fire.

📍 Long Beach, CA
All 13 Aeon R engines are installed on the thrust structure and are moving through integrated gimbal testing, validating their ability to pivot precisely to steer and stabilize the vehicle during flight.

From tank integration to engine production, September builds kept the team busy.

✓ Installed the downcomer into the stage 1 flight tank  
✓ All primary hardware on the stage 1 aft dome is complete, closing in on final integration 
✓ Interstage drilling finished, now heading to the Tender Loving Crusher for structural testing 
✓ First 2 ground station controllers stood up
✓ First welds complete for the Aeon V vacuum engine nozzle extension 
✓ Flights 2 and 3 engines well into manufacturing with production ramping

From the downcomer going into the stage 1 tank to stage 2 completing its wet dress rehearsal at Stennis, September brought progress across every discipline.

🔩 Build: The downcomer was installed into the stage 1 flight tank. The interstage completed drilling and was passed off to the Tender Loving Crusher ahead of structural testing. Engine production continues to ramp, with articles for flights 2 and 3 well into manufacturing.
🧪 Test: With all 13 engines installed, the thrust structure transitioned into integrated gimbal testing. At Stennis, stage 2 completed a wet dress rehearsal on the A2 stand, building towards the first hot fire test.
🏗️ Launch: The east lightning protection tower reached its full height of 530 feet, the east launch table structural steel is complete, and permanent 480-volt power has been energized at the pad.

This morning at #IAC2026, ispace Founder & CEO Takeshi Hakamada joined the plenary discussion “Navigating the Cislunar Crossroads: Partnerships, Security and Japan as a case study,” moderated by Charlotte Nassey, Senior Government Affairs & Policy Lead at @ispace_EUROPE.

As activity around the Moon continues to grow, the panel explored how international cooperation, interoperability, and standardization of interfaces can shape a resilient and sustainable cislunar ecosystem.

"The Moon is a blank page. You can imagine anything you want, and that inspires innovation," said Hakamada-san as the session closed. 🌙
